title: http-grpc-streaming-benchmarks
summary: Investigation and benchmark notes comparing HTTP (chunked, SSE) and gRPC streaming behavior for our serving runtime. Focus areas: per-chunk overhead, backpressure handling, proxy impacts (Envoy/ALB/nginx), TLS/keepalive, and client-side chunking strategies. High-level takeaways and recommended config defaults included.
content:
Purpose:
This doc collects experiments and observations about networking/streaming overheads for Redwood's serving runtime. We want to quantify the per-chunk and per-request overhead for HTTP vs gRPC streaming, measure how proxies affect tail latency and throughput, and validate backpressure behavior for continuous token streaming workloads (LLM chat/generation).

Scope:
- Protocols: HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2 (SSE and chunking similarities), gRPC (HTTP/2, unary/streaming).
- Proxies: Envoy (HTTP/2 multiplexing + gRPC fusion), ALB (AWS), nginx (HTTP/1.1/2), simple TCP passthrough.
- Client chunking strategies: per-token, n-token batches (4/8/16), fixed-size bytes (e.g., 256B), and server-driven flush.
- TLS and keepalive/connection reuse.
- Load shapes: single-hot (1k QPS, large concurrency), steady-state (sustained 200-1000 RPS), bursty (sudden spikes and recovery).

Testbed:
- Model runtime: local serving runtime instance (cpu/gpu offload disabled for pure network testing) pinned to 8 vCPU, 16GB RAM, simulated token production with deterministic delays (50ms per chunk baseline).
- Clients: custom harness written in Go, wrk2 for HTTP, ghz for gRPC, and a NodeJS SSE client for browser-like behavior.
- Proxies deployed in front of the runtime in the same VPC/subnet. TLS termination tested both at proxy and at origin.
- Observability: Prometheus (request duration, active streams), p95/p99 latency across chunk/stream boundaries, kernel TCP metrics (sndbuf/backlog), and packet captures for a subset.

Key metrics collected:
- Time-to-first-byte (TTFB) for first chunk and subsequent chunks.
- Chunk inter-arrival latency and jitter under load.
- End-to-end latency for complete response.
- CPU and context-switch overhead on client and server when streaming at high concurrency.
- Request/stream failure modes under backpressure (timeouts, connection resets, 429/503).

Representative runs (high level):
1) Baseline (no proxy, TLS disabled):
   - Per-chunk overhead (software flush + network): ~3-5ms on local loopback, 8-12ms over VPC.
   - gRPC streaming slightly better for small frequent chunks: p50 delta -1ms vs HTTP/1.1 chunked, p99 comparable.
   - When client sends per-token flush (i.e., 1 token ~= 20-50 bytes), overhead dominates: throughput low and CPU on server increases (many syscalls). Recommendation: avoid per-token flush in production.

2) Envoy in front (HTTP/2, h2 mux enabled):
   - Observed head-of-line improvements for multiplexed streams, but tail latency increases when Envoy worker threads saturate.
   - Envoy adds ~2-6ms median to per-chunk delivery; p99 impact larger under high concurrent streams (10-25ms extra).
   - gRPC benefits from HTTP/2 multiplexing when many concurrent streams use fewer connections; Envoy config tuning (per-worker concurrency, buffer limits) necessary.

3) ALB (AWS) in front:
   - ALB terminates TLS and upgrades to HTTP/1.1 or 2 depending on client. ALB imposes coarser flow control causing larger chunk batching (good for cost) but increases latency jitter and p99 by 20-50ms in bursty scenarios.

4) nginx as reverse-proxy (proxy_buffering on/off):
   - proxy_buffering on: nginx buffers small chunks and emits larger packets: improved throughput and lower server CPU, but adds addtl buffering latency (40-120ms depending on buffer config).
   - proxy_buffering off: more immediate forwarding but increases packets/syscalls and server CPU; latency lower median but tail suffers under concurrent load.

Backpressure behavior:
- gRPC streaming: backpressure propagates via HTTP/2 flow control windows; good for preventing overrun at the transport layer. Observed graceful slowdown when client reader is slow.
- HTTP/1.1 chunked: no transport-level multiplexed flow control; server can overwhelm client if not careful. HTTP/2 (SSE on h2) mitigates this but proxy/proxy_buffering settings can break flow-control semantics.
- When using Envoy with http2, we saw cases where Envoy's internal buffering masked upstream backpressure and caused memory pressure before applying downstream stalls. Tuning envoy.buffer_limits and upstream_connection_options is critical.

Chunk size experiments (per-chunk bytes):
- Per-token (~30-100 bytes): worst throughput, highest syscall/CPU overhead. p99 large.
- 256B chunks: decent latencies; good tradeoff for interactive latency and efficiency.
- 1-4KB chunks: best throughput and CPU efficiency, but increases time-to-first-intermediate when model produces tokens slowly.
Recommendation: default to 256-512B chunking at the SDK level, with option to increase for batch-heavy workloads.

TLS and keepalive:
- TLS handshake adds a large one-time cost; always favor connection reuse and HTTP/2 long-lived connections.
- Keepalive settings on proxies and server influence how quickly we can recover from transient client disconnects. Short TCP timeouts with aggressive connection churn cause more TLS handshakes and increase p99.

Client-side strategies and SDK guidance:
- Avoid per-token flush by default. Buffer small tokens for up to 50-100ms or until 256B threshold to amortize syscall overhead.
- Use HTTP/2/gRPC where possible for browsers that support h2; otherwise use SSE/websockets for browser fallback.
- Provide SDK config knobs: chunk_size_bytes, max_buffer_time_ms, enable_http2 (fallback order).

Proxy-specific recommendations:
- Envoy: increase worker threads and tune buffer limits when large numbers of concurrent streams are expected. Set cluster.http2_options.max_concurrent_streams appropriately. Enable downstream flow control to honor upstream backpressure.
- nginx: disable proxy_buffering for strictly low-latency interactive sessions if resource limits can handle increased CPU. Otherwise enable buffering with conservative buffer sizes.
- ALB: where possible, avoid using ALB for ultra-low-latency interactive workloads; consider TCP passthrough or regional NLB with TLS at origin.

Open issues / TODOs:
- Repeat tests with real model runtime (generation timings vary) instead of deterministic token delay to capture variance due to compute spikes.
- Measure memory pressure on Envoy with thousands of concurrent streams (we did up to 2k but need 10k+).
- Validate browser SSE and websocket fallbacks at scale (we only tested 200 concurrent browser clients).
- Evaluate connection pooling strategies at SDK level for high-churn serverless user workloads.

Conclusions (short):
- gRPC streaming generally yields lower per-chunk overhead and better flow-control semantics (recommended for server-to-server).
- HTTP streaming (chunked/SSE) is acceptable for browser clients but needs careful proxy configs and client-side chunking to avoid high tail latency and CPU overhead.
- Proxies add non-trivial p99 overhead and can mask backpressure; tune buffer limits aggressively and prefer TCP passthrough when latency critical.
- SDK-level sensible defaults (256-512B chunking + short buffer window) improve efficiency without harming interactivity.

Next actions:
- Implement SDK default chunking config and a toggle for per-token flush. Owner: eng-dx (Priya).
- Add Envoy config presets to infra repo for streaming workloads (Liam).
- Re-run benchmarks with production models and scale targets (Ava).

Notes to reviewers:
- See linked artifacts for raw CSVs and ghz/wrk scripts. Raw perf artifacts are in the benchmarks subfolder of the repo.
- Comments inline for anything missing or experiments you think should be prioritized.
